LESSON 77 OF 106·Social Engineering and the Human Factor

Building a Reporting Culture and Reporting Channels

Why reporting is the highest-value control you have, what makes a channel get used, and how to design one that people trust — including your own, as an individual.

Foundation14 min
Why this matters

You cannot defend against what nobody tells you about. A reporting rate that is implausibly low is a signal about the culture, not about the absence of incidents.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

Architecture & Trust Boundary Flow

Interactive mental model for Building a Reporting Culture and Reporting Channels: compare normal operation, boundary failure, and defensive design.

  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.
  2. Weakness: Check how many people used the reporting channel last month, and whether that number moves at all.
  3. Impact: The component trusts unverified data, crossing a confidentiality or integrity boundary.
01 Untrusted Input
Enforced control
02 Server Policy Gate
Verified
03 Verified Operation
  1. Verification: Make reporting one action, available from email and from the tool bar, with no justification required.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.
  3. Resilience: Invalid requests fail closed and emit structured security telemetry.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Every report is free information, and every suppressed report is an incident you will learn about later and more expensively.
  • People hide mistakes when the response to a mistake is worse than the response to an incident.
  • The reporting channel has to be easier than the alternative of saying nothing.
  • Reports need to be acted on visibly, or the channel dies.
  • Time to report is itself a security metric, because it drives how many victims there are.

The background

  • Reporting was rare and often treated as an admission of failure, which suppressed exactly the information defenders needed.
  • Awareness programmes began to include reporting as an explicit objective rather than a secondary benefit.
  • Phishing report buttons made reporting a single action, which raised volumes sharply.
  • Organisations matured to treating reported events as the normal input to detection engineering rather than as a problem.

Real-world examples

  • A user who clicked a link and did not report it means an entire campaign succeeds because of one non-report.
  • A team with a low report rate usually has low trust, and often has more incidents than a team with a high one.
  • A reported suspicious email is often a compromise of somebody else account, so one report protects many people.

What to look for

  • Check how many people used the reporting channel last month, and whether that number moves at all.
  • Check what happens to a person after a report, and whether anyone has asked.
  • Check whether there is a channel that does not require opening a ticket or talking to a manager.
  • Check whether reports are fed back to the people who made them.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Phishing attacks: defending your organisation

Reading the reporting-culture layer of a national authority's guidance, including why users who fear reprisals stop reporting mistakes

Open NCSC resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Make reporting one action, available from email and from the tool bar, with no justification required.
  • Respond to reports with a visible outcome, even when the outcome is that it was harmless.
  • Train explicitly that reporting a mistake early is the behaviour being wanted.
  • Measure report volume, time to report and report quality, and treat a drop as a warning.
  • Give the security team the authority to act on a report without a management approval step.
